newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sea of white balloons sweeps through Brussels.
newsitem.headline: Sea of white balloons sweeps through Brussels.

text.p: A sea of white swept through Brussels on Sunday as over a quarter of a million people swept through the streets bearing what has become a sign of national protest in Belgium - white, the colour of purity.
The so-called White March, officially in support of the six victims of a paedophile gang, also targets what is widely seen as a corrupt political and judicial system.
Marchers brandished white balloons, flowers and caps or wore white clothes as they took part in Belgium's biggest-ever demonstration.
From balconies along the way plain white banners flew and balloons bobbed in a chill wind.
But despite the demonstrators' obvious pent-up anger, the march was going peacefully.
One organiser, Paul Marchal, father of An Marchal who died while in the hands of the child molesters, kidnappers and murderers, told the marchers, "Keep your fists in your pockets."

The rally follows an initiative by the parents of the four dead children -- Julie Lejeune, Melissa Russo, Eefje Lambrecks and An Marchal -- and those of two missing girls -- Elisabeth Brichet and Loubna Benaissa.

Under the eye of the world's media, marchers from Belgium and neighbouring countries -- estimated to total more than 275,000 -- focused on their concern for the future, particularly for their children, and on the need for justice.
Marchal said the march was "for our children, and yours."

In line with the wishes of the parents there were few banners or placards with slogans. Politicians, seeking to avoid accusations of exploiting the event for party-politics, stayed on the sidelines, commenting on the march on radio and TV only.
One analyst said on VTM television, "this demonstration is a supreme expression of the people's views."

Corine de Lanckner said, "All the things going here -- it is too much. For years we stayed silent, just nodding our heads. Our anger is growing now. Justice must be for the people, for everyone, not just for people with money or power."

Belgian media have repeatedly alleged there was high-level police, judicial and political involvement in the paedophile ring, said to have been part of an international network, but proof has yet to emerge.
Marie-Noelle Bouzet, mother of missing girl Elisabeth Brichet, said on RTL television, "the criminals are much better organised than the authorities."
Some shops along the route from Brussels' North Station to its South Station, had posters in their windows proclaiming, "Stop the cover-up operation by the Gendarmerie and the courts."
